Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A ruler for rotating spacetime Take the stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat Kerr vacuum metric as a supplied exact solution. Set electric charge to zero and neglect disc and test-particle self-gravity. Use G = c = M = 1: restore physical lengths with GM/c² and times with GM/c³. Let χ = cJ/(GM²) be nonnegative and label the orbital direction separately. Σ = R² + χ² cos²θ, Δ = R² − 2R + χ² ds² = −(1−2R/Σ)dt² − (4χR sin²θ/Σ)dt dφ + (Σ/Δ)dR² + Σdθ² + [R²+χ²+2χ²R sin²θ/Σ]sin²θ dφ² The mixed coefficient is 2gₜφ. Setting χ = 0 recovers Schwarzschild. R is a Boyer–Lindquist coordinate, not an areal radius when the spin is nonzero. We derive consequences of the metric; its construction from the Einstein equations is left to the references. 02Separate the horizon and static limit The outer horizon is the larger root of Δ = 0. An observer at fixed R, θ, and φ has ds² = gₜₜdt² and can be timelike only where gₜₜ < 0. The outer root of gₜₜ = 0 defines the static limit. R₊ = 1 + √(1−χ²) Rₑ(θ) = 1 + √(1−χ²cos²θ) The surfaces meet at the poles; the equatorial static limit remains at R = 2. Between them static observers are impossible, but rotating timelike observers can exist. The static limit is not a no-escape boundary. The panel stays in the exterior and does not evolve horizon-crossing or exactly extremal orbits. 03Allowed angular velocities and frame dragging Hold R and θ fixed and rotate at Ω = dφ/dt. Substitution into the metric gives a quadratic that must be negative. Its null endpoints bound the allowed angular velocities of stationary timelike observers. gₜₜ + 2gₜφΩ + gφφΩ² < 0 Ω₋ < Ω < Ω₊, Ω± = [−gₜφ ± √(gₜφ²−gₜₜgφφ)]/gφφ ΩZ = −gₜφ/gφφ = 2χR / [(R²+χ²)²−χ²Δsin²θ] Even zero angular momentum pφ = gₜφuᵗ + gφφuφ generally requires a nonzero ΩZ. This describes frame dragging of a locally nonrotating observer. Such a fixed-radius observer generally needs acceleration; ΩZ is not the angular velocity of a freely orbiting particle. 04From circular orbits to the ISCO For a massive equatorial test particle, conserved specific energy E and angular momentum L separate the radial motion. The Carter constant vanishes in the equatorial plane. Combine the two circular-orbit conditions with marginal radial stability. Σ²(dR/dτ)² = ℛ(R) ℛ = [E(R²+χ²)−χL]² − Δ[R²+(L−χE)²] ℛ = ∂Rℛ = ∂²Rℛ = 0 ⇒ R² − 6R + 8sχ√R − 3χ² = 0 Differentiate at fixed E and L, then eliminate them. Set s = +1 for prograde and s = −1 for retrograde motion. Selecting the physical exterior branch yields the closed expression below. Z₁ = 1 + (1−χ²)1/3[(1+χ)1/3+(1−χ)1/3] Z₂ = √(3χ²+Z₁²) RISCO,s = 3+Z₂−s√[(3−Z₁)(3+Z₁+2Z₂)] At χ = 0 both branches give six. As χ approaches one, the prograde limit is one and the retrograde limit is nine. This does not place an ordinary timelike orbit on the exactly extremal horizon. Infall can occur inside the ISCO; pressure and magnetic stresses make a disc inner edge a different question. 05Compare different spins Curves show coordinate radii computed from the equations, not an observed shadow or integrated trajectories. Changing inputs compares stationary spacetimes; it is not a time evolution of a spinning-up black hole. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If the equatorial static limit stays at R = 2 while the horizon moves inward, what changes? Show the answer and reasoning An exterior ergoregion opens up. It forbids static timelike observers, rather than escape itself; permitted stationary timelike motion must co-rotate. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
